reason: Start with the outer route that carries sound to the eardrum.
expectation: The eardrum will fit at the inner end of the ear canal, ready to receive vibrations.

alternatives.reason: Building the cochlear sensory structure also looks useful, but I prefer to follow sound inward.

effect: The eardrum now closes the canal, so I can continue along the sound-transmitting route.
reaction: The fitting was straightforward and matched the picture.
reason: Attach the ossicles to carry eardrum movement onward toward the cochlea.
expectation: The ossicle chain will connect to the eardrum, with its stapes end available for the cochlea.

effect: The ossicles now connect the eardrum to the stapes, so the inner-ear structures are next.
reaction: The smaller stapes footplate makes the transfer toward fluid more concrete.
reason: Fit the cochlear membranes into the fluid chambers to build the next part of the sound path.
expectation: The basilar and tectorial membranes will occupy the cochlear partition, leaving room for sensory cells.

alternatives.reason: Connecting hair cells to nerve fibres also advances the sensory route, but I want to build their surroundings first.

effect: The cochlear membranes are in place, but the sensory-cell layer is still missing.
reaction: The base-to-apex view makes the structure easier to place, though its function is not yet explained.
reason: Add the hair cells to the cochlear membranes before connecting their nerve fibres.
expectation: The sensory epithelium will fit between the membranes, positioning its hair bundles to respond to movement.

alternatives.reason: Connecting the hair cells to nerve fibres is also useful, but fitting them into the cochlea comes first in my plan.

effect: The sensory epithelium is positioned on the basilar membrane, with its nerve-contact side exposed for the next connection.
reaction: The exposed contact makes the next step clear.
reason: Connect the auditory nerve fibres; it is the only offered combination.
expectation: The fibres will connect to the hair cells and provide a route for signals toward the brain.

effect: The cochlea now has a nerve connection; hair cells signal chemically to fibres that generate action potentials.
reaction: The distinction between graded hair-cell voltage and nerve spikes is useful.
reason: Join the mechanical and sensory paths; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: The stapes will meet the cochlear window, linking sound transmission to the sensory structures.

effect: The stapes now meets the oval window, joining the sound-transmitting route to the sensory cochlea.
reaction: The free round window is a useful detail, though its role is not yet explained.
reason: Connect the completed ear to the body and brain; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: The cochlear nerve will connect toward the brain, completing the hearing pathway.
